Pandemic Related Academic Impact in 2021
What do state summative assessments tell us
Damian Betebenner & Adam Van Iwaarden
Center for Assessment

CCSSO Assessment Directors Meeting
September 21st, 2021

Pandemic Related Academic Impact
• As we are all aware, the pandemic greatly disrupted the lives of
people worldwide over the last 18 months.
• The impact on education was dramatic with millions of students
receiving education in new ways.
• A concern of many is to what extent the pandemic impacted
students: Academically, emotionally, physically.
• The Center has been working with a dozen states to investigate the
extent to which the pandemic has impacted student learning.
• My colleagues and I wrote a blog detailing some early findings:
https://www.nciea.org/blog/covid-19-disruptions/assessing-
academic-impact-covid-19-summer-2021

Pandemic Related Academic Impact
• The pandemic and all the ensuing disruptions functions as a kind of
“academic headwind”, impeding (in general) the academic progress of
students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
• They slow one’s rate of progress
• The slower rate of progress leads to less distance being travelled.
• In education these two outcomes represent themselves as:
• Decrease in student growth.
• Decrease in student attainment.
• Special consideration must be given to accommodate low participation/
changing demographics (multiple imputation and propensity score
matching)

Pandemic related academic impact
• Understanding pandemic related impact necessarily requires looking
back to pre-pandemic results.
• The impulse of stakeholders to want to compare 2021 results with 2019
results is the correct impulse at both the individual, school, district, and
state level.
• Wanting to look at 2019 to 2021 change is an attempt to investigate
impact.
• The challenge is making 2019 to 2021 comparisons apples-to-apples
comparisons.
• Supporting these comparisons requires having a complete
understanding is who constitutes the missing data. More on that after
some initial comparisons.

Data to assess academic impact
• During the 2020-2021 academic year, student achievement data from
achievement vendors (primarily Renaissance Star, NWEA MAP, and Curriculum
Associates iReady) was all that was available to investigate pandemic related
academic impact.
• States summative assessments (cancelled in 2020) were broadly administered
nationwide in 2021.
• Participation rates ranged from normal (> 95%) to poor.
• Given their technical quality, alignment with state standards, coverage of the
state student population, and long-term history, for nearly all states, 2021
state summative assessment data provides excellent data on which to begin
investigating academic impact.
• Many states have ELP assessments from 2020 as 2021 with which to
investigate academic impact on the ELL subgroup.

Analyses for 2020-2021
• With comparable results we can quantify pandemic related
academic impact:
• At the state level
• Demographic subgroups including ethnicity, poverty
• Academic subgroups (special education, low/high achievers)
• By region/district/school
• By mode of education (remote/hybrid/in-person).
• Attendance
• English Language Learner impact can be evaluated using WIDA-ACCESS
results.
CCSSO State Assessment Directory September 2021 Meeting

Student attainment
• Across the dozen states we’ve examined thus far:
• Decreases in percent proficient are most often reported (thought
percent proficient can mask changes in the distribution)
• Decreases in ELA generally in the upper single digits but sometimes in the teens.
• Decreases in Math generally in the lower teens.
• In terms of mean scale score decreases, effect sizes are large ranging
from 0.2 to 0.4.
• These are large effect sizes, especially when seen at the state level.

CCSSO State Assessment Directory September 2021 Meeting

Student growth
• States we’ve worked with utilize SGPs to measure growth.
• States created baseline growth norms using pre-pandemic
student data.
• By grade/content area median SGPs in ELA between low 40s to
low 30s. In Mathematics between mid 30s to low 20s.
• Academic impact by grade is relatively uniform.
• These decreases in student learning (i.e., growth) corroborate
losses seen in attainment.
• Decreases of this magnitude in student learning will likely require
multiple years

Demographic/Academic Subgroup Impact
• By ethnicity, academic impacts are, in general, relatively uniform.
• Asian students showed slightly larger impacts in mathematics
• ELL status on state summative show fairly uniform academic
impact.
• On ELP assessments, larger impact in lower grades than in middle/
upper school grades.
• Special education/IEP status in some states showed lesser impact
that their non-special education counterparts
• In middle school mathematics, several states show higher
achievers demonstrating larger impacts than low achievers.

Demographic/Academic Subgroup Impact
• States collecting data of mode of education during the pandemic
(e.g., in-person, hybrid, remote) show more impact for students
receiving remote instruction versus in-person instruction.
• Given these findings many states have prioritized efforts to get
students back to in-person learning as quickly and safely as
possible.

Looking forward to 2021-2022
• As we (hopefully) transition from pandemic to recovery, data from
2021-2022 will provide an excellent basis to understand whether what
type of recovery systems are demonstrating:
• V-shaped, U-Shaped, L-Shaped, or no recovery
• States with compromised 2021 assessments (low participation, fall
testing, no testing) will have tradeoffs to make in terms of using
2021-2022 data to assess recovery.
• Using data for these purposes is not the typical use of data for
“accountability” and requires states to promote results in ways not
related to accountability. This can be a delicate balancing act.
• Overall, I’m optimistic about the use of 2020-2021 data for academic
impact as well as to inform recovery in 2021-2022.
